label: explain-track-2
one_line: We test whether a published formula for how fast a ring of gut bacteria spreads in jelly holds on data it never saw.
what: Track 2 studies a ring of living bacteria. The bacteria are E. coli, spread from one spot in a dish of soft jelly. The ring moves outward at a steady speed, a few millimetres each hour. A published formula says how that speed should depend on how fast the cells divide. We write down what the formula predicts before we open the measurements. Then we compare. We also fit a very simple rule as a baseline. Our aim is not a new fact about bacteria. It is a fair, repeatable check of a named rule, with an honest record of where it holds and where it breaks.
why: Scientists often write a rule for how a living pattern forms. Few check that rule on data they did not use to build it. This track is a small, clean test of that habit. The bacteria are only a test case. If the rule fails, we say so. If it holds only in some conditions, we say which ones. The same method can then be reused on other patterns.

steps.text: Pick the system. Gut bacteria spread from a spot in soft jelly that is loose enough for cells to swim through.
steps.picture: A drop of ink in thin gel, except the ink is alive and can steer.

steps.text: Name what we measure. One number is how fast the outer edge moves, in millimetres per hour. The other is how fast the cells divide.
steps.picture: The speed of a spreading crowd, and how quickly the crowd is having babies.

steps.text: Understand the effect. When the jelly holds a little food-like chemical, the cells make a ring at the edge. They eat the chemical, which makes a slope, and they swim up it.
steps.picture: A crowd following a smell trail that it lays down itself.

steps.text: Set the plain-spreading baseline. Cells that only grow and wander would spread at a known, slower speed.
steps.picture: A slow walk in a random direction, used as the speed to beat.

steps.text: Write down the formula. It says speed grows with the square root of the division rate, and does not depend on how fast cells eat the chemical.
steps.picture: A recipe card that says which dials matter and which do not.

steps.text: Fit a simple rule on six normal measurements. It says speed squared is a fixed multiple of the division rate.
steps.picture: A rule of thumb with no biology in it, used as a bar to clear.

steps.text: Write the predictions down and date them before opening the unseen measurements.
steps.picture: Sealing your guess in an envelope before the race.

steps.text: Open the unseen data and compare. Record each prediction as holding, failing, or too uncertain to say.
steps.picture: Opening the envelope and marking it in front of everyone.

steps.text: Check the checkers. Others recompute our sums from the public files, and we check how strict each pass-or-fail rule really is.
steps.picture: A second person re-weighing the ingredients.

wrong_if: Here is the bet, written before looking. If the formula is right, doubling the division rate should raise the speed by only about 41 percent. That is the square-root rule. Earlier project numbers hint that the real effect is closer to a straight doubling. If the unseen data show an effect near that, with a range of doubt that excludes the square-root value, then the formula is wrong for this system. We have not yet seen enough data to say, and one set of points so far is too weak to settle it.
could_go_wrong: The unseen data are only unopened by us; the paper figures may already show them, so the test is not fully blind.
Some pass-or-fail rules are looser than the noise in the data, so a right formula could fail and a wrong one could pass.
One key measurement rests on only two or three dishes per point, so its range of doubt is wide.
Every experiment we use has the same jelly firmness, and speed drops sharply when the jelly gets firmer, so firmness is a hidden factor.
A 2024 study found that the older model fails when cells are very crowded, and our data may sit in that zone.
That 2024 study used a narrow channel, not jelly, so we do not know whether its finding carries over.
Some numbers depend on our reading of units in a file that does not state them.
The formula's exact form was checked only in the paper text, not re-derived by us.

questions.q: How do you know the ring really is faster than plain spreading?
questions.a: The paper reports that steering along a self-made slope speeds the ring up. Our own sums agree: the measured speeds are 2.49 to 7.59 times the plain-spreading speed across 25 conditions.

questions.q: How do you know your sums are right?
questions.a: Independent checkers re-ran them from the public files. The slopes, the baseline fit and the speed ratios came out the same.
We did not re-derive the formula from the paper's equations. We did not open the large image archive. We did not test other labs, because we found no public data from a fully independent lab.

questions.q: Why not just use the data to fit the formula?
questions.a: A rule tuned on the data will always fit it. Only a prediction made first can fail, and a test that can fail is worth something.
Only partly. It fits six normal measurements, then lands within 15 percent on just 7 of 17 others. The errors run from 7.8 to 94 percent.
Yes. A 2024 paper says the usual model breaks at high cell density, and proposes a fix. It tested a narrow channel, so how well it fits jelly is unknown.

questions.q: Does our rule library already cover this?
questions.a: No. The library has no checked law for steered fronts. The nearest one, for plain spreading, is still a candidate. It gives only a lower bound on speed.

questions.q: Is the new square-root law proven?
questions.a: A computer checked the maths of the statement. That shows the algebra is sound. It does not show real colonies obey it.

glossary.plain: A common bacterium that lives in the gut of people and animals.
A jelly made from seaweed, so loose that bacteria can swim through it.
The outer edge of the spreading colony, seen as a moving ring.
A chemical, like a faint smell of food, that cells swim towards.
Swimming up or down a chemical slope.
How fast an amount changes from one place to the next.
How quickly the cells divide.
The number that gives your number when multiplied by itself; the square root of 4 is 2.
A short written rule that links numbers to each other.
A simple rule used as the bar that a better idea must beat.
A result we write down before looking at the data.
Measurements we keep unopened so they can test a prediction fairly.
Spread by dividing and wandering at random, with no steering.
The known speed of a front driven only by growth and random wandering.
A rule in our library that is not yet fully accepted.
The span of values the data cannot rule out.
Something that changes the result but is not tracked in the data.
A set of equations that stands in for a real system.
How tightly packed the cells are.
A crowd of bacteria grown from one starting spot.
Our list of rules whose maths a computer has checked line by line.
A computer program that checks mathematical proofs line by line.
A saved set of measurements.
A thousandth of a metre, about the thickness of a coin.
Slow random spreading, like a smell drifting through a room.

check_yourself.what: Check the first source paper exists and has the title shown
check_yourself.expect: The title Chemotaxis as a navigation strategy to boost range expansion.

check_yourself.what: Find the square-root sentence in the second paper
check_yourself.command: curl https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8640786/fullTextXML and search for 'square root dependence on the growth rate'
check_yourself.expect: A sentence in the results section that says speed depends on the square root of the growth rate.

check_yourself.what: Redo the baseline fit and the speed ratios
check_yourself.expect: A fitted constant of 16.904, and 7 of 17 other conditions within 15 percent.

check_yourself.what: Compare the plain-spreading speed with the measured one
check_yourself.expect: Ratios from 2.49 to 7.59 times the plain-spreading speed.

check_yourself.what: Check the Phan 2024 claim about crowded cells
check_yourself.expect: An abstract saying the older model breaks down at high cell densities.

check_yourself.what: Confirm our law library has no steered-front law

left_out: Phan 2024 as the 'strongest' rival: only partly supported, so it is described as a rival, not the best one.
The claim that every frozen number is correct and the problem is only the rules: only partly supported, so it is not stated as a fact.
That one prediction (the e-fold length) is 'sound' with a 1 percent correction and 3 to 5 percent spread: not recomputed by the checkers, so left out.
Power figures for the speed-independence test and the claim that a plateau test cannot fail: the agent's own analysis, only partly checked.
The 150 MB size cap and which predictions need the big image archive: project rules, not checkable, so not given as fact.
The advice to keep, add or drop particular datasets: a recommendation, not a checkable claim.
Median ratio of 4.73 and the 4.4 to 5.4 wild-type ratios: not in the verified list, so only the 2.49 to 7.59 range is used.
The 6-of-14-within-15-percent figure: not verified, so the checked 7-of-17 figure is used instead.
